segments.voice: Yesterday, a week of work ended with Karma Yoga's ideal: the silence of the desert in the middle of the busiest street.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `A DESERT IN THE BUSY STREET.`

segments.voice: Nobody asks a chemistry student to take the textbook on faith. Sooner or later there's a lab, a pair of goggles, and a teacher saying, don't trust me, watch what happens. Vivekananda opened his book Raja Yoga with that kind of offer, made about the mind. Last week asked how you find the quiet in the middle of work. This book is his answer, and it starts by asking you not to believe him yet.
screen: `A TEXTBOOK, OR A LAB?` → `DON'T TRUST ME, WATCH.` → `A BOOK ABOUT THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Raja Yoga is his book on the yoga of the mind. Its second half carries his rendering of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the text this path met much earlier, the one that opens: now, the teaching of yoga. The first half is his own teaching, and it begins with an argument. The great teachers of religion, he says, did not only believe. They saw. They spoke of what they had perceived for themselves. And if one person has perceived something, he says, others can perceive it too, given the right method. So religion, in his telling, shouldn't rest only on someone else's report. It can be tested by experience, the way a science is. Raja Yoga offers a practical method for that testing, and it asks for no belief at the start. Try it, and see what you find. Then the twist. The lab isn't somewhere else. The instrument is the mind itself, and the first problem is that it doesn't hold still long enough to observe anything. So before any great experience, the book gets very practical: posture, breath, and above all, learning to watch and gather the mind. Karma Yoga said do your work and let go of what comes. Raja Yoga turns around and studies the one doing the work. Same teacher. A different door into the same house.
screen: `THE TEACHERS DIDN'T ONLY BELIEVE; THEY SAW.` · `WHAT ONE PERSON PERCEIVES, OTHERS CAN.` · `TEST IT, DON'T JUST BELIEVE IT.` · `THE LAB IS THE MIND ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Treat this sit as a first experiment: back upright but easy, the breath at its own pace, nothing to reach. Every few breaths, ask quietly what your mind is doing right now, planning, remembering, listening, drifting, answer honestly with one word, and go back to the breath. If you pray, you can begin or end with a prayer you already know.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's book on the yoga of the mind, which asks you to test before you believe.
Your line: the lab is the mind itself. Tomorrow, the experiment meets a monkey. That's day nine hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Vivekananda's Raja Yoga is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers, often alongside Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, and students describe starting with posture, breath and watching the mind.
